title: Design a Hotel Reservation System — Object Model
prompt: Design the object model for a hotel reservation system. Users search for available rooms for a date range, book a room, pay, and can cancel. The system must never double-book a room for overlapping dates. Design the core classes, the availability/booking model, the reservation lifecycle, and pricing. Focus on class design and APIs rather than the distributed backend. Sketch the class diagram.
blurb: Availability over date ranges without double-booking, a reservation state machine, and pluggable pricing.

rubric.label: Requirements clarification
rubric.description: Separates functional (search by dates, book, pay, cancel, room types) from non-functional (no double-booking, availability correctness, extensible pricing).

rubric.label: Core entities
rubric.description: Hotel, Room, RoomType, Reservation, Guest, DateRange, Payment, Inventory/Availability — cleanly separated.

rubric.label: Class design & responsibilities
rubric.description: Availability is its own concept over a DateRange; Room vs RoomType distinction; Reservation owns its lifecycle.

rubric.label: Relationships & cardinality
rubric.description: Hotel 1..* Room; RoomType groups Rooms; Reservation references a Room/RoomType + DateRange + Guest. Composition vs association reasoned.

rubric.label: Design patterns
rubric.description: State for reservation lifecycle, Strategy for pricing (seasonal/dynamic), Repository for storage, optionally Observer for confirmations.

rubric.label: SOLID / OCP
rubric.description: New pricing rule or room type plugs in without editing Reservation; availability logic isolated.

rubric.label: API / method design
rubric.description: searchRooms(dateRange, type), book, confirm, cancel, checkIn/Out, isAvailable — clear signatures.

rubric.label: Reservation state machine
rubric.description: Explicit states + legal transitions; cancellation and no-show handled; guards enforced.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Overlapping-date conflict, same-day checkout/checkin boundary, cancellation policy windows, payment failure after hold, over-search inventory.

rubric.label: Concurrency
rubric.description: Two guests booking the last room for overlapping dates; holds/locks; idempotent booking. THE core challenge.

rubric.label: Extensibility
rubric.description: Multiple hotels, amenities, loyalty pricing, group bookings, overbooking policy added cleanly.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Narrates availability model and state diagram, states tradeoffs, reasons about the double-booking race.

functional_requirements: Search rooms available for a given date range and room type
Book a specific room/room-type for a date range for a guest
Pay for the reservation; hold inventory during checkout
Cancel a reservation subject to a cancellation policy
Room types with different capacities, amenities, and prices
nonfunctional_requirements: A room is never double-booked for overlapping dates — the hard invariant
Availability queries are correct and reasonably fast
clarifying_questions: Do guests book a specific room or just a room type (inventory of N)?
Single property or a chain of hotels?
Is check-in date inclusive and check-out exclusive (a room frees on checkout day)?
What's the cancellation policy — free window, partial refund, non-refundable rates?
Do we allow overbooking to hedge no-shows?
Pricing model — fixed, seasonal, or dynamic by occupancy?

core_classes.name: Hotel
core_classes.responsibility: A property with rooms and a pricing policy.

core_classes.name: RoomType
core_classes.responsibility: A category (Standard/Deluxe/Suite) with capacity, amenities, base price.

core_classes.name: Room
core_classes.responsibility: A physical bookable unit of a RoomType.

core_classes.name: DateRange
core_classes.responsibility: Value object for [checkIn, checkOut); provides overlap test.

core_classes.name: Availability / InventoryCalendar
core_classes.responsibility: Tracks, per room or room-type, which date ranges are taken; answers isAvailable and holds dates.
key_fields: Map<roomId, Set<DateRange>> booked  // or per-day counts per type

core_classes.name: Reservation
core_classes.responsibility: A booking: guest, room/type, date range, price, and lifecycle state.

core_classes.name: ReservationState
core_classes.responsibility: State pattern base; concrete states define legal transitions.

core_classes.name: PricingStrategy
core_classes.responsibility: Abstract: compute total for a room type + date range (seasonal/dynamic).

core_classes.name: CancellationPolicy
core_classes.responsibility: Determines refund based on time-to-checkin and rate type.

core_classes.name: BookingService
core_classes.responsibility: Orchestrates search → hold → pay → confirm; enforces the no-double-book invariant.

relationships: Hotel composes Rooms and defines RoomTypes; each Room is-a instance of one RoomType (association).
Reservation references one Room (or RoomType inventory slot), one Guest, one DateRange, and composes a Payment and ReservationState.
Availability/InventoryCalendar is the single source of truth for what's taken; BookingService mutates it under a lock.
BookingService depends on PricingStrategy, CancellationPolicy, PaymentGateway abstractions (DIP).

design_patterns.why: Localizes legal transitions and guards; e.g. can't check in a cancelled reservation.
Pricing and refund rules vary independently and plug in without editing Reservation (OCP).
Abstracts persistence and enables the atomic availability check.
Encapsulates the interval math the whole design depends on.

apis: book(guestId, roomType, dateRange) -> Reservation (state PENDING, inventory held)
state_transitions: PENDING → CONFIRMED (payment succeeds) | EXPIRED (hold TTL elapses) | CANCELLED
CONFIRMED → CHECKED_IN (arrival) | CANCELLED (per policy) | NO_SHOW (didn't arrive)
CANCELLED, EXPIRED, NO_SHOW, CHECKED_OUT are terminal
Guards: can't check in before CONFIRMED; can't cancel after CHECKED_IN
edge_cases: Two guests book the last matching room for overlapping dates → exactly one succeeds
Check-out day == another booking's check-in day → not an overlap ([in, out) half-open)
Payment fails after inventory hold → release the hold on timeout
Cancellation inside the free window (full refund) vs after (penalty) vs non-refundable rate (no refund)
Search returns a room that gets booked before this user checks out → re-validate at book time
Duplicate book request from a retry → idempotency key
concurrency: THE core problem: prevent double-booking overlapping dates. Options: pessimistic lock on the room/room-type row while checking availability + inserting; a unique constraint on (room_id, date) or a range-exclusion constraint; or an atomic conditional insert.
Hold pattern: reserve inventory with a short TTL during checkout, commit on payment, auto-release on timeout to avoid inventory leaks
Availability read must be consistent with the write that commits the booking
extensibility: Chain of hotels → Hotel is one aggregate; search spans properties
Overbooking policy → allow N+k holds per type, strategy-controlled
Group bookings / room blocks → reserve multiple rooms atomically
Amenities and add-ons → composed onto RoomType/Reservation

deep_dives.probe: Two users try to grab the last deluxe room for July 4–6. Walk me through the exact mechanism that guarantees only one wins. Lock, unique constraint, or atomic conditional write — pick one and defend it.
How do you represent availability so isAvailable(room, range) is correct and fast? Per-day rows, interval set, or occupancy counts per type? What are the tradeoffs?
A user holds a room during checkout but abandons the payment. How do you avoid leaking that inventory forever? Describe the hold/commit/release lifecycle.
Is check-out day bookable by the next guest? Model the interval so a same-day turnover isn't a false conflict.
Model free-window vs penalty vs non-refundable so adding a new rate type doesn't touch Reservation.

followup_bank.trigger: mentions available or availability or search
followup_bank.question: How is availability stored so overlap checks are correct — per-day rows, interval set, or per-type counts?
Two people book the last room for overlapping dates at the same instant. What exact mechanism makes one fail?
If a user holds a room then vanishes, how does that inventory get released? What's the TTL story?
Model the refund so a new non-refundable rate type doesn't require editing Reservation.
Is checkout day an overlap with the next checkin? How does your DateRange handle the boundary?

tradeoffs: Book specific room (deterministic, less flexible) vs book room-type inventory (flexible, assign room at check-in)
Pessimistic lock (simple, correct, contention) vs unique/exclusion constraint (DB-enforced, elegant) vs optimistic retry
Per-day availability rows (simple overlap) vs interval sets (compact, trickier)
Holds with TTL (no leaks, more moving parts) vs book-then-pay (simpler, risk of no-pay bookings)
reference.reference_answer: A strong mid-level answer treats availability as a first-class concept over a half-open DateRange, distinguishes Room from RoomType, and centers the design on the no-double-book invariant — enforced by a pessimistic lock on the room/type while checking-and-inserting, or better, a database unique/exclusion constraint on (room, date). It uses a hold/commit/release pattern with a TTL so abandoned checkouts don't leak inventory, models the reservation lifecycle as a State machine with guards, and extracts pricing and cancellation into Strategy objects. It gets the [checkIn, checkOut) boundary right so same-day turnover isn't a false conflict, and makes booking idempotent. Signal: naming a concrete concurrency mechanism rather than hand-waving 'we lock it.'

interviewer_notes: This is the mid-level bar, so the concurrency invariant — never double-book — is the make-or-break. Let them build the entities, then present 'two users grab the last room for overlapping dates' and insist on a concrete mechanism (lock, unique/exclusion constraint, or atomic conditional write), not 'we'll lock it.' Check they distinguish Room from RoomType and get the half-open date boundary right (checkout day is bookable). Probe the hold/TTL pattern for abandoned checkouts. Pricing and cancellation as strategies is a plus but secondary. Keep them out of infra weeds — this is object design.
